title: B. F. Skinner: Reinforcement Theory
overview: B. F. Skinner did not offer a personality theory. He tried to explain all behavior by what can be observed, measured and controlled, treating people as 'empty organisms' whose behavior is caused by external consequences rather than inner states. Working with rats and pigeons, he distinguished respondent behavior (elicited by stimuli, as in Pavlov's conditioning) from operant behavior (emitted, acting on the environment and controlled by reinforcement). He saw personality as a collection of reinforced operant behaviors. The chapter covers his life, operant conditioning in the Skinner box, schedules of reinforcement, shaping by successive approximation, superstitious behavior, techniques of self-control, and applications such as token economies and behavior modification, including why he preferred positive reinforcement to punishment. It also covers his deterministic image of human nature, functional analysis and the assessment of behavior, his single-subject research, criticisms including instinctive drift, and his decline in influence after the rise of cognitive psychology.
objectives: Explain how Skinner's behavioral approach differs from other personality theories, including the idea of the 'empty organism'.
Describe how Skinner's life experiences relate to his view of behavior.
Distinguish respondent from operant behavior and explain conditioning, reinforcement and extinction.
Describe operant conditioning in the Skinner box and its application to personality.
Compare the four schedules of reinforcement with continuous reinforcement.
Explain shaping by successive approximation and the origin of superstitious behavior.
Describe the four self-control techniques and the research on benefits of self-control.
Explain token economies, behavior modification, punishment and negative reinforcement.
Outline Skinner's position on questions of human nature.
Describe functional analysis and the three methods of assessing behavior, and evaluate Skinner's research approach, criticisms and current status.

sections.heading: Rats, Pigeons, and an Empty Organism
sections.detailed:
Skinner is the odd one out in a personality textbook. He never proposed a personality theory, and his research was not aimed at personality at all. He wanted to explain all behavior, not just personality, using only factual, descriptive terms. In his view psychology had to stay with facts: what can be seen, manipulated and measured in the laboratory. In practice that meant studying only the overt responses an organism makes. For Skinner, psychology is simply the science of behavior, of what an organism does.

Because of this, the chapter calls his work the antithesis (direct opposite) of the psychoanalytic, trait, life-span, cognitive and humanistic approaches. It differs from them in subject matter, in methods and in aims. Those theorists explain personality by looking inside the person. They point to causes, motives and drives that originate within each individual and steer development and behavior.

Skinner made no use of internal, subjective states to explain behavior. Unconscious influences, defense mechanisms, traits and other inner driving forces cannot be observed, so he argued they have no place in a scientific psychology. He said they are worth no more to science than the old theological idea of the soul. It is important for exams to note that he did not deny that such inner forces exist. He denied only that they are useful for science.

He applied the same reasoning to physiological processes. They are not overtly observable either, so they too are irrelevant to a science of behavior. He described the inside of the organism as irrelevant, whether as the site of physiology or of mental activity (quoted in Evans, 1968). This is the meaning of his description of people as "empty organisms": nothing inside us can explain behavior in scientific terms. The causes of behavior lie outside the person, in the environment and in the consequences that follow behavior. The chapter's opening quotation sums this up: it is the environment that must be changed.

The behavioral approach therefore rests on three commitments. First, the subject matter is observable behavior only. Second, the method is controlled laboratory experimentation. Third, the explanation is always external: environmental stimuli and the reinforcers that follow responses.
sections.simple: Skinner did not offer a personality theory. He thought psychology should study only behavior that can be seen and measured. Inner things like the unconscious, traits or even brain processes cannot be observed, so he left them out of science. That is why he called people "empty organisms".
keyPoints: Skinner offered no personality theory; he tried to explain all behavior in factual, descriptive terms.
Psychology is the science of overt behavior: what can be seen, manipulated and measured.
Internal states (unconscious, defenses, traits) were rejected as useless for science, though not denied to exist.
Physiological processes were also treated as irrelevant because they are not overtly observable.
"Empty organism": nothing inside the person explains behavior scientifically; causes are external.

sections.heading: Where Are the People?
sections.detailed:
Skinner also differed from other theorists in his choice of research subjects. Some personality theorists built their ideas on emotionally disturbed patients and others on normal, average people. Abraham Maslow based his theory on the best and brightest. Skinner's behavioral research used rats and pigeons, although his ideas were later applied to people.

He justified this choice in several ways. First, he was interested in behavioral responses to stimuli, not in childhood memories or adult feelings. Responding to stimuli is something animals do well, sometimes better than humans. Second, he admitted that human behavior is more complex than animal behavior. But he held that the difference is one of degree, not of kind, because the fundamental processes are similar. Third, a science must move from the simple to the complex, so the more elementary processes should be studied first. Animal behavior is simpler, so it was the logical place to start.

Even though his research was on animals, his work has had wide practical use in changing human behavior. Behavior therapy techniques derived from his research are used in clinical settings to treat disorders including psychoses, mental retardation (the book's term) and autism. Behavior-modification techniques are widely used in schools, businesses, correctional institutions and hospitals. This answers the obvious question, "what can pigeons teach us about people?": the same principles of reinforcement turned out to work on human behavior in real settings.
sections.simple: Skinner studied rats and pigeons instead of people. He believed animal and human behavior differ only in degree, and that science should study simple processes first. His findings were later used widely to change human behavior in clinics, schools and workplaces.
keyPoints: Skinner's subjects were rats and pigeons, unlike theorists who studied patients, normal people or (Maslow) the best and brightest.
His interest was responses to stimuli, which animals display well.
Human and animal behavior differ in degree, not kind; the basic processes are similar.
Science proceeds from simple to complex, so simpler animal behavior was studied first.
His work led to behavior therapy and behavior modification in clinics, schools, businesses, prisons and hospitals.

sections.heading: The Life of Skinner (1904–1990): A Strict Childhood, Machines and Animals, A Dark Year
sections.detailed:
A strict childhood. B. F. Skinner was born in Susquehanna, Pennsylvania, the older of two sons. His younger brother died at 16. His hardworking parents kept setting out clear rules of proper behavior, and he said he was raised to fear God, the police and what people would think. His mother never relaxed her strict standards and controlled him with a disapproving "tut tut". His grandmother made sure he understood the punishments of Hell by pointing to the red-hot coals in the parlor stove. His father taught him what happens to criminals by showing him the county jail and taking him to a lecture on life in a notorious New York state prison.

In his autobiography Skinner described how these warnings shaped him as an adult. When he visited a cathedral, he took care not to step on the gravestones in the floor, because as a child he had been told again and again that this was improper. Experiences like this convinced him that his adult behavior had been determined by the rewards and punishments (the reinforcements) he had received in childhood. The chapter therefore argues that his system, and his view of people as complex systems behaving in lawful ways (Skinner, 1971), reflected his own early life.

Machines and animals. As a child Skinner spent many hours building mechanical devices: wagons, seesaws, carousels, slingshots, model airplanes, and a steam cannon that fired potato and carrot plugs over neighbors' houses. He also tried to build a perpetual-motion machine, which, as the book jokes, perpetually failed. This tinkering foreshadowed his view of people as machines that operate predictably. His interest in animals also began in childhood. He kept turtles, snakes, toads, lizards and chipmunks. At a county fair he was fascinated by performing pigeons that raced onstage, pulled a toy fire engine to a burning building, put a ladder against it, and climbed up (one wearing a fireman's hat) to rescue a stranded pigeon. As an adult he trained pigeons to play Ping-Pong and to guide a missile to its target. He taught his daughters' cat to play the piano and his Beagle to play hide and seek.

A dark year. Skinner majored in English at Hamilton College in upstate New York and expected to become a novelist. He set up a study in the attic of his parents' home in Scranton, Pennsylvania, but the writing never came. He read, listened to the radio, played the piano and built ship models while waiting for inspiration. He thought of seeing a psychiatrist, but his father said it would be a waste of money. At 22 he was a failure at the one thing he wanted to do. He later called this his dark year, which the chapter likens to what Erikson called an identity crisis. His occupational identity as a writer collapsed and took his self-worth with it. A move to Greenwich Village in New York City did not help his writing. Several women also rejected his declarations of love, and he was so upset that he branded one woman's initial on his arm, where it stayed for years (Skinner, 1983).
sections.simple: Skinner grew up with strict parents and grandparents who used warnings and threats of punishment. He came to believe his own adult habits were produced by these childhood rewards and punishments. He loved building machines and keeping animals. After college he failed as a novelist, a period he called his dark year.
keyPoints: Born in Susquehanna, Pennsylvania; strict family taught him to fear God, the police and others' opinions.
Childhood warnings (e.g., not stepping on gravestones) persuaded him that behavior is determined by past reinforcements.
Building gadgets foreshadowed his view of people as predictable machines; pets and fair pigeons sparked his animal interest.
Majored in English at Hamilton College; failed as a novelist at 22, his 'dark year', likened to Erikson's identity crisis.
Rejection in love led him to brand a woman's initial on his arm.

sections.heading: The Life of Skinner: A New Identity, A Period of Depression, and Quirky, Conscientious, and Somewhat Neurotic
sections.detailed:
A new identity. Just as he was losing hope, Skinner found an identity he kept for the rest of his life. He decided that writing had failed him, not the other way round, and that he would study human behavior with the methods of science instead of fiction. He read Pavlov and Watson and committed himself completely to behaviorism. He entered Harvard in 1928 to study psychology without ever having taken a course in it, and he earned his Ph.D. in three years.

Choosing behaviorism meant rejecting the feelings and emotions he had tried to draw on as a writer. The historian Mindess (1988) contrasted the two careers. Fiction depends on inspiration, intuition, free association, the stream of consciousness, the unconscious, fantasies and feelings. Behaviorism dismisses that whole inner world as "pre-scientific" and attends only to observable behavior and how to record, predict and control it. The chapter notes that psychic processes appeared in Skinner's work only to be mocked.

A period of depression. Supported by postdoctoral fellowships, Skinner stayed at Harvard until 1936. He then taught at the University of Minnesota and Indiana University and returned to Harvard in 1947. In his 40s he went through a period of depression. He resolved it by going back to his failed identity as a writer and producing the novel Walden Two (1948). Its main character voices Skinner's own personal and professional frustrations. The book is still in print and has sold more than two million copies. It describes a society in which every part of life is controlled by positive reinforcement, the basic principle of his psychology (Altus & Morris, 2009). Adams (2012) suggested that Walden Two anticipated major themes of the later positive psychology movement.

Quirky, conscientious, and somewhat neurotic. Early in his career Skinner agreed to take both the Rorschach and the Thematic Apperception Test. In 2012 a group of Norwegian psychologists analysed his results (Overskeid, Gronnerod, & Simonton, 2012; Gronerod, Overskeid, & Hartmann, 2013; Koren, 2013). They rated him high in conscientiousness and openness to experience, somewhat extraverted, and neurotic. They also described him as quirky and driven in his work, with strained social relationships and a lack of liveliness. One of his daughters, however, called him a wonderful father who spent a great deal of time with his children (Freeman, 2013).

Into his 80s Skinner kept working with enthusiasm. He regulated his habits, recording his daily work output and the average time he spent per published word, which was 2 minutes. He thus became a living example of his own definition of humans as complex systems behaving in lawful ways. He once told a friend that he was cited in the psychology literature more often than Freud. Asked whether that had been his goal, he answered that he thought he might make it (quoted in Bjork, 1993).
sections.simple: Skinner turned from fiction to science, read Pavlov and Watson, and got a Harvard Ph.D. in three years. In his 40s he beat depression by writing Walden Two, a novel about a society run on positive reinforcement. Later analysis of his projective tests described him as conscientious, open, quirky and somewhat neurotic. He worked into his 80s and kept careful records of his own output.
keyPoints: Committed to behaviorism after reading Pavlov and Watson; entered Harvard in 1928 and earned a Ph.D. in three years.
Behaviorism meant rejecting feelings, fantasies and the unconscious as 'pre-scientific' (Mindess).
Depression in his 40s resolved by writing Walden Two (1948), a society controlled by positive reinforcement.
Norwegian analysis of his Rorschach and TAT: high conscientiousness and openness, somewhat extraverted, neurotic, quirky.
Recorded his own output (2 minutes per published word), living out his idea of humans as lawful systems.

sections.heading: Reinforcement: The Basis of Behavior
sections.detailed:
Skinner's approach is simple in concept, but it rests on thousands of hours of carefully controlled research. Its central idea is that behavior is controlled by its consequences, that is, by what follows it. Skinner believed that an animal or a person could be trained to do almost anything, and that the kind of reinforcement following the behavior would determine it.

The social implication is significant and often examined. Whoever controls the reinforcers has the power to control human behavior, just as an experimenter controls the behavior of a laboratory rat. This places the cause of behavior wholly outside the person, in the pattern of consequences supplied by the environment, parents, teachers, employers and governments.

Skinner then separated two kinds of behavior, respondent and operant, explained in the next sections. Both depend on reinforcement, but they differ in how they are produced and whether they change the environment.
sections.simple: Skinner's key idea is that what happens after a behavior controls whether it happens again. With the right reinforcement, almost any behavior can be trained. So whoever controls the rewards controls the behavior.
keyPoints: Behavior is controlled by its consequences, by what follows it.
Almost any act can be trained; the type of reinforcement determines the behavior.
Whoever controls the reinforcers controls behavior, as an experimenter controls a rat.
Skinner distinguished respondent from operant behavior.

sections.heading: Respondent Behavior (Conditioning, Reinforcement, Extinction)
sections.detailed:
Respondent behavior is a response made to, or elicited by, a specific stimulus. The simplest kind is reflexive, such as the knee jerk: a tap on the knee (stimulus) produces a jerk of the leg (response). This behavior is unlearned. It happens automatically and involuntarily, and we need no training or conditioning to make it.

Conditioning. At a higher level is respondent behavior that is learned. This learning, called conditioning, involves substituting one stimulus for another. The concept came from the Russian physiologist Ivan Pavlov in the early 1900s, and John B. Watson later adopted Pavlov's ideas as the basic research method of behaviorism. Pavlov noticed that his dogs salivated to neutral stimuli such as the sound of their keeper's footsteps, although salivation had earlier been produced only by the sight of food. He then studied this systematically by sounding a bell shortly before feeding a dog. At first the dog salivated only to the food, because the bell meant nothing. After a number of bell-then-food pairings, the dog salivated to the bell alone. It had been conditioned: its response had shifted from the food to a formerly neutral stimulus.

Reinforcement. Pavlov's experiment showed the importance of reinforcement. The dogs would not learn to respond to the bell unless they were rewarded for doing so, and here the reward was food. Pavlov stated a basic law of learning: a conditioned response cannot be established without reinforcement. Reinforcing a response strengthens it and makes it more likely to be repeated.

Extinction. A conditioned response will also not be maintained without reinforcement. Suppose the experimenter keeps ringing the bell but stops giving food. Each time the bell sounds and nothing follows, the dog's salivation drops in frequency and intensity until it disappears. This is extinction: the response is wiped out because the reinforcement has stopped. Much research shows that the more reinforcement is given during training, the more resistant the conditioned response is to extinction (Shull & Grimes, 2006). Eventually, however, extinction does occur.

Exam tip: respondent behavior is elicited by a known stimulus, depends on reinforcement, and does nothing to change the environment. This is the contrast with operant behavior.
sections.simple: Respondent behavior is a reaction that a particular stimulus pulls out of us, like a knee jerk. Pavlov showed that a dog could learn to salivate to a bell paired with food, which is conditioning. The response forms only if it is reinforced, and it fades away (extinction) when reinforcement stops.
keyPoints: Respondent behavior is elicited by a specific stimulus; reflexes like the knee jerk are unlearned and involuntary.
Conditioning (learned respondent behavior) substitutes one stimulus for another (Pavlov; adopted by Watson).
Pavlov's dogs came to salivate to a bell after repeated bell-food pairings.
Pavlov's law: no conditioned response can be established without reinforcement.
Extinction: withholding reinforcement eliminates the response; more reinforcement in training gives more resistance to extinction.

sections.heading: Operant Behavior
sections.detailed:
Respondent behavior depends on reinforcement and is tied directly to a physical stimulus, so each response is elicited by a specific stimulus. Skinner considered respondent behavior less important than operant behavior. We are conditioned to respond to many stimuli, but this cannot explain all behavior. Much human behavior seems spontaneous and cannot be traced to any particular stimulus. Such behavior is emitted, not elicited. It looks voluntary rather than an involuntary reaction to a conditioned stimulus.

Operant behavior is behavior emitted spontaneously or voluntarily that operates on the environment and changes it. Its nature and frequency are determined or modified by the reinforcement that follows it.

The key contrast concerns the environment. Respondent behavior has no effect on the environment: the salivation of Pavlov's dog did not change the bell or the food that followed it. Operant behavior acts on the environment and changes it as a result. The word 'operant' itself means that the organism operates on its surroundings.

Comparison for exams. Respondent behavior is elicited by a known stimulus, is often reflexive or involuntary, and leaves the environment unchanged; the knee jerk and the dog salivating to a bell are examples. Operant behavior is emitted with no identifiable eliciting stimulus, appears voluntary, changes the environment, and is controlled by the consequences that follow it; the rat pressing a bar for food is the example. Skinner considered operant behavior far more important for understanding human behavior.
sections.simple: Operant behavior is behavior we give out on our own, not something a stimulus pulls out of us. It changes the world around us, and what happens afterwards (reinforcement) decides how often we repeat it. Skinner thought this kind of behavior mattered much more than respondent behavior.
keyPoints: Operant behavior is emitted, not elicited; it appears spontaneous and voluntary.
Its nature and frequency are determined by the reinforcement that follows it.
Respondent behavior does not change the environment; operant behavior operates on it and changes it.
Skinner rated operant behavior as more important than respondent behavior.

sections.heading: Operant Conditioning and the Skinner Box
sections.detailed:
Operant conditioning is the procedure by which a change in the consequences of a response affects the rate at which the response occurs. Skinner illustrated it with his operant-conditioning apparatus, known as the Skinner box (Figure 12.1).

A food-deprived rat placed in the box at first behaves spontaneously and randomly: it is active, sniffing, poking and exploring. These behaviors are emitted, not elicited, because the rat is not responding to any particular stimulus. At some point during this random activity, it presses a lever or bar on one wall, and a food pellet drops into a trough. Its behavior has operated on the environment and changed it, since the environment now contains food. The food is a reinforcer for bar pressing.

The rat begins pressing the bar more often, gets more food, and presses still more. Its behavior is now under the control of the reinforcers. Its activity becomes less random because it spends most of its time pressing and eating. If the rat is put back the next day, we can predict its behavior and control its bar pressing by presenting or withholding reinforcers, or by presenting them at a different rate. Withholding food extinguishes operant behavior just as it extinguishes respondent behavior: a behavior that no longer brings a reward eventually stops. So whoever controls the reinforcers controls the subject's behavior.

From the Skinner box to the real world. Many animals have been taught complex behaviors through operant conditioning. Dogs have been conditioned to sniff out drugs or explosives. Giant African rats in Mozambique have been trained to detect buried land mines. Lobsters have learned to grasp a bar with their claws to get food. Whales and dolphins perform tricks at places like SeaWorld, and calves have been taught to urinate only in designated places (Gillaspy, Brinegar, & Bailey, 2014; Poling et al., 2010; Tomina & Takahata, 2010; Vaughan et al., 2014).
sections.simple: In the Skinner box, a hungry rat happens to press a lever and gets food. Because the food follows the press, the rat presses more and more, and its behavior comes under the control of the food. Stop the food and the pressing dies out. The same method has trained dogs, rats, lobsters, dolphins and calves to do useful tasks.
keyPoints: Operant conditioning: changing the consequences of a response changes its rate.
In the Skinner box, a random bar press produces food, which reinforces further pressing.
The experimenter can predict and control behavior by presenting, withholding or re-timing reinforcers.
Withholding reinforcement extinguishes operant behavior too.
Real-world uses: drug and explosive dogs, mine-detecting rats in Mozambique, lobsters, dolphins, calves.

sections.heading: Operating on the Environment
sections.detailed:
Skinner believed that most human and animal behavior is learned through operant conditioning. Babies show how. An infant first produces random, spontaneous behaviors, and only some of them are reinforced by parents, siblings or caregivers, for example with food, hugs or toys. As the child grows, the positively reinforced behaviors that parents approve of persist. Those the parents disapprove of are extinguished.

The principle is the same as for the rat in the Skinner box. Behaviors that work, such as pressing the bar for food, are shown often, and behaviors that do not work are dropped. The relationship runs both ways. The organism's behavior operates on the environment, and the environment, in the form of reinforcement, operates back on the behavior.

This shows how powerful reinforcement can be. Skinner (1953) compared operant conditioning to a sculptor shaping a lump of clay. If the organism needs the reinforcer badly enough, there is almost no limit to how its behavior can be shaped. The shaper might be an experimenter with a food pellet, a puppy owner with a dog biscuit, a mother with a smile, a boss with a pat on the back, or a government with a promise.
sections.simple: Babies do lots of random things, and the ones parents reward stick while the rest fade. Behavior changes the environment, and the environment's rewards change behavior back. If someone needs a reward badly enough, their behavior can be shaped almost without limit.
keyPoints: Most human and animal behavior is learned through operant conditioning.
Infants' reinforced behaviors persist; unreinforced or disapproved ones are extinguished.
Two-way process: behavior operates on the environment, and reinforcement operates on behavior.
Operant conditioning shapes behavior as a sculptor shapes clay; reinforcers range from food pellets to a government's promise.

sections.heading: Personality: A Collection of Operant Behaviors
sections.detailed:
From infancy we emit many behaviors, and those that are reinforced grow stronger and form patterns. This is how Skinner understood personality: as a pattern or collection of operant behaviors, not as an inner structure or set of traits.

The same view explains abnormality. What other psychologists called neurotic or abnormal behavior was, for Skinner, nothing mysterious. It was simply the continued performance of undesirable behaviors that had somehow been reinforced. This implies that changing the reinforcement can change abnormal behavior, which is the logic of behavior modification later in the chapter.

Having shown that behavior could be changed by continuous reinforcement, that is, giving a reinforcer after every response, Skinner asked what would happen if he varied the rate of reinforcement. This led to his work on schedules of reinforcement.
sections.simple: For Skinner, personality is just the set of behaviors that have been rewarded and have become habits. 'Abnormal' behavior is simply unwanted behavior that has somehow been rewarded. He then asked what happens if behavior is rewarded only some of the time.
keyPoints: Personality = a pattern or collection of operant behaviors that have been reinforced.
Neurotic or abnormal behavior = undesirable behavior that has somehow been reinforced.
Continuous reinforcement means a reinforcer after every response.
Skinner next varied the rate of reinforcement, which led to schedules of reinforcement.

sections.heading: Schedules of Reinforcement: Fixed Interval and Fixed Ratio
sections.detailed:
Skinner noted that outside the laboratory behavior is rarely reinforced every time it happens. Babies are not picked up every time they cry. Baseball stars do not hit a home run at every at-bat. A supermarket bagger is not tipped for every bag, and a favorite band does not win a Grammy for every song. Yet these behaviors persist on occasional reinforcement. Skinner also observed that his rats kept pressing at a fairly steady rate even when not every press was reinforced. He therefore tested different reinforcement schedules, meaning patterns or rates of providing or withholding reinforcers, to see how well they control behavior. The four he tested were fixed interval, fixed ratio, variable interval and variable ratio.

Fixed interval (FI). The reinforcer is given for the first response that occurs after a fixed period of time has passed, such as 1 or 3 minutes. Timing has nothing to do with the number of responses. Whether the rat presses 3 or 20 times a minute, the reinforcer comes only after the set time has elapsed and the correct response is made. A job paid weekly or monthly works this way: pay depends on the time worked, not on the number of items made or sales closed.

Skinner found that the shorter the interval between reinforcers, the more often the animal responded, and response rate fell as the interval grew longer. How often reinforcers came also affected how quickly the response could be extinguished. The response stopped sooner when a continuously reinforced rat lost its reinforcement than when an intermittently reinforced rat did. FI schedules have proved highly effective in real situations, including special education classrooms, where they reduced disruptive behavior (Tomlin & Reed, 2012).

Fixed ratio (FR). Reinforcers are given only after a set number of responses, for example every 10th or 20th. Unlike FI, reinforcement here depends on how often the subject responds: the rat gets no pellet until it has made the required number of presses. FR produces a faster rate of responding than FI, and this holds for humans too. In piece-rate work, earnings depend on how much is produced. A salesperson on commission earns more by selling more. By contrast, a salesperson on a weekly salary is on an FI schedule and earns the same regardless of sales.
sections.simple: Real-life behavior is usually rewarded only some of the time. On a fixed-interval schedule, the reward comes for the first response after a set time, like a monthly salary. On a fixed-ratio schedule, the reward comes after a set number of responses, like piece-rate pay or commission, and this makes people respond faster.
keyPoints: Reinforcement schedules are patterns or rates of providing or withholding reinforcers; Skinner tested FI, FR, VI and VR.
Fixed interval: reinforcement for the first response after a fixed time (weekly or monthly salary).
Shorter FI intervals give higher response rates; continuous reinforcement extinguishes faster than intermittent.
FI has reduced disruptive behavior in special education classrooms (Tomlin & Reed, 2012).
Fixed ratio: reinforcement after a set number of responses (piece-rate, commission); faster responding than FI.

sections.heading: Schedules of Reinforcement: Variable Interval and Variable Ratio
sections.detailed:
Everyday life does not always allow fixed schedules, so reinforcers often come on a variable basis.

Variable interval (VI). The time between reinforcers varies. The reinforcer might come after 2 hours the first time, after 1 hour 30 minutes the next, and after 2 hours 15 minutes the third. Someone fishing all day is rewarded, if at all, on a VI basis, because the schedule depends on fish biting at random times.

Variable ratio (VR). Reinforcement is based on an average number of responses between reinforcers, with wide variation around that average. Skinner found VR very effective at producing high and stable response rates, which, the book notes, casino operators can confirm. Slot machines, roulette wheels, horse races and state lotteries all pay on VR schedules, an extremely effective way to control behavior.

General conclusions. Variable schedules produce lasting responses that tend to resist extinction. Most everyday learning happens on variable-interval or variable-ratio schedules. Overall, Skinner's research showed that reinforcement schedules are effective for controlling, modifying and shaping behavior. Anyone in charge of rats, salespeople or assembly-line workers, or training a pet or a child, can use these techniques to produce the behavior they want.

Quick comparison of all five. Continuous: every response is reinforced; learning is quick, but extinction is also quick. FI: reinforcement after a fixed time; response rate rises as the interval shortens. FR: reinforcement after a fixed number of responses; faster than FI. VI: reinforcement after varying times. VR: reinforcement after a varying number of responses around an average; high, stable and very resistant to extinction.
sections.simple: On a variable-interval schedule, the reward comes after unpredictable amounts of time, like waiting for a fish to bite. On a variable-ratio schedule, the reward comes after an unpredictable number of tries, like a slot machine. Variable schedules make behavior very persistent and hard to extinguish, and most everyday learning happens this way.
keyPoints: Variable interval: reinforcer after varying time periods (fishing).
Variable ratio: reinforcer after a varying number of responses around an average (slot machines, roulette, lotteries).
VR produces high, stable response rates.
Variable schedules produce lasting behavior that resists extinction; most everyday learning is VI or VR.
Schedules can be used to control, modify and shape behavior in workers, pets and children.

sections.heading: The Shaping of Behavior (Successive Approximation; Shaping a Person in Five Minutes)
sections.detailed:
In Skinner's original experiment the operant behavior, pressing a lever, is simple. A rat exploring at random is likely to do it eventually, given a patient experimenter. But animals and people show many complex operant behaviors that are very unlikely to occur in the normal course of events. How can a pigeon or a child be conditioned to perform behaviors it would probably never produce on its own?

Successive approximation. Skinner's answer was successive approximation, or shaping (Skinner, 1953). He trained a pigeon to peck a particular spot in its cage, something it was unlikely to do by chance. First, the pigeon was reinforced with food simply for turning toward the spot. Then reinforcement was withheld until it made some movement, however slight, toward the spot. Next, only movements that brought it closer were reinforced. After that, it was reinforced only for thrusting its head toward the spot, and finally only when its beak touched the spot. This sounds slow, but Skinner conditioned pigeons this way in less than 3 minutes.

The procedure explains the name. The organism is reinforced as its behavior, in successive or consecutive stages, comes closer and closer to the final desired behavior. Successive approximation is therefore the chapter's explanation of how complex behavior is acquired.

Learning to speak. Skinner suggested that children learn the complex behavior of speaking in this way. Infants spontaneously make meaningless sounds, which parents reinforce by smiling, laughing and talking. After a while parents reinforce the babbling differently, giving stronger reinforcers for sounds that resemble real words. As the process continues, parental reinforcement becomes more selective and is given only for correct usage and proper pronunciation. Language is thus shaped by differential reinforcement in stages.

Shaping the behavior of a person in five minutes. Skinner once shaped the behavior of the psychoanalyst Erich Fromm, whose comments in a lecture annoyed him, especially when Fromm argued that people are not pigeons. Skinner passed a note to a colleague saying he would shape a chopping motion of Fromm's left hand. Whenever Fromm's left hand rose, Skinner looked straight at him. When the hand came down, he nodded and smiled. Within five minutes Fromm was chopping the air so vigorously that his wristwatch kept slipping over his hand (Skinner, 1983). Attention and approval served as reinforcers, showing that shaping works on people even without their awareness.
sections.simple: Shaping, or successive approximation, means rewarding small steps that get closer and closer to the behavior you want. Skinner taught pigeons to peck a spot this way in under 3 minutes. Children learn to speak the same way, as parents reward babbling, then word-like sounds, then correct words. Skinner even shaped Erich Fromm's hand gestures during a lecture just by nodding and smiling.
keyPoints: Complex, low-probability behaviors are learned by successive approximation (shaping).
Pigeon example: reinforce turning toward the spot, then movement toward it, head thrust, and finally a beak touch; done in under 3 minutes.
Reinforcement is given at successive stages as behavior approximates the final desired behavior.
Speech is shaped by parents' increasingly selective, differential reinforcement of babbling, word-like sounds and correct words.
Skinner shaped Erich Fromm's left-hand chopping motion within five minutes using looks, nods and smiles.

sections.heading: Superstitious Behavior (How to Shape Superstitious Behavior)
sections.detailed:
Life is not as orderly as a laboratory. Sometimes we are reinforced by accident just after doing something. That behavior did not cause the reinforcement in any way, yet it may be repeated in similar situations. Skinner called this superstitious behavior: persistent behavior that has a coincidental, not a functional, relationship to the reinforcement received.

Football examples. A Tampa Bay Buccaneers offensive lineman having a terrible season early in his career asked his roommate to switch beds so he could sleep nearer the bathroom. His play immediately improved, and for the rest of his career he insisted on the bed nearest the bathroom door in every motel. An NFL kicker hugged the goal posts before each game because he had once done so just before a successful kick. He said he wanted the posts to know he loved them and to stay still when he kicked.

How to shape superstitious behavior. Skinner showed this in the laboratory. A hungry pigeon in the apparatus was reinforced every 15 seconds on a fixed-interval schedule. The pigeon was almost certainly doing something when each pellet arrived: turning, raising its head, strutting, hopping or standing still. Whatever it was doing at that moment was reinforced. Skinner found that a single reinforcement was enough to make the pigeon repeat the accidentally reinforced behavior more often for a while. That raised the chance that the next pellet would arrive during the same behavior. With short intervals between reinforcers, superstitious behaviors are learned quickly.

As with the footballers, the pigeon's behavior has no functional link to the reinforcer; the connection is unintentional. In humans, such behaviors may last a lifetime and need only occasional reinforcement to keep them going. The chapter summary adds that superstitious behavior arises when reinforcement is presented on a fixed- or variable-interval schedule.

Research. A study of major league baseball players in the United States and Japan found that 74 percent admitted to superstitious behavior. American players were more superstitious than Japanese players, suggesting that culture may influence the extent of such actions (Burger & Lynn, 2005).
sections.simple: Superstitious behavior happens when a reward arrives by coincidence right after some action, so we keep repeating that action even though it did nothing. Skinner fed pigeons every 15 seconds no matter what, and they kept repeating whatever they happened to be doing at feeding time. Athletes' rituals work the same way. A study found 74 percent of baseball players had superstitions.
keyPoints: Superstitious behavior: persistent behavior with a coincidental, not functional, link to reinforcement.
Examples: lineman insisting on the bed nearest the bathroom; NFL kicker hugging the goal posts.
Lab demo: hungry pigeon reinforced every 15 seconds (FI); whatever it was doing got repeated.
One reinforcement is enough; short intervals speed learning; in humans occasional reinforcement can sustain it for life.
Burger & Lynn (2005): 74% of US and Japanese baseball players superstitious; Americans more so.

sections.heading: The Self-Control of Behavior (Stimulus Avoidance, Self-Administered Satiation, Aversive Stimulation, Self-Reinforcement)
sections.detailed:
For Skinner, behavior is controlled and modified by variables outside the organism. No process, drive or other internal activity determines it. Even so, he allowed that we can exercise self-control, which he described as acting to alter the impact of external events. Self-control is the ability to exert control over the variables that determine our behavior. He did not mean control by some mysterious inner 'self'. He meant that, to some extent, we can manage the external variables that control us. He described four techniques.

1. Stimulus avoidance. We remove ourselves from an external variable that affects our behavior. If a noisy roommate is disturbing your study before a morning exam, you can go to the library. By avoiding a person or situation that makes you angry, you reduce the control it has over you. Similarly, alcoholics can avoid a stimulus that controls their drinking by not keeping liquor in their homes.

2. Self-administered satiation. We cure ourselves of a bad habit by overdoing the behavior. A smoker who wants to quit can chain-smoke for a time, inhaling until he or she becomes so disgusted, uncomfortable or sick that quitting follows. This technique has worked in formal therapeutic programs designed to eliminate smoking.

3. Aversive stimulation. We arrange unpleasant or repugnant consequences for failing. Obese people who want to lose weight might announce their plan to friends in person or to a larger audience on Facebook or other social networking sites. If they do not keep their resolution, they face the unpleasant consequences of personal failure, embarrassment and criticism.

4. Self-reinforcement. We reward ourselves for good or desirable behavior. A teenager who commits to reaching a certain grade point average, or to looking after a younger brother or sister, might reward himself or herself with concert tickets or new clothes.

The crucial point for Skinner is that external variables still shape and control behavior. But sometimes, through our own actions, we can modify how those external forces affect us. Self-control in his system is therefore not free will. It is a person rearranging their own environment and consequences.
sections.simple: Skinner said behavior is controlled from outside, but we can partly control those outside forces ourselves. We can avoid tempting situations, overdo a bad habit until we are sick of it, set up embarrassing consequences for failing, or reward ourselves for doing well. Self-control is about rearranging our environment, not an inner willpower.
keyPoints: Self-control: the ability to exert control over the external variables that determine our behavior; not a mysterious 'self'.
Stimulus avoidance: leave or remove the controlling stimulus (go to the library; keep no liquor at home).
Self-administered satiation: overdo the habit until it becomes aversive (chain-smoking); used in anti-smoking programs.
Aversive stimulation: arrange unpleasant consequences for failure (public announcement of a weight-loss goal).
Self-reinforcement: reward yourself for desirable behavior (concert tickets for reaching a target GPA).

sections.heading: Benefits of Self-Control
sections.detailed:
The chapter reports several findings on the value of self-control. A large-scale study of American college students found that those scoring high on a measure of self-control had better grades, higher psychological adjustment, and more self-acceptance and self-esteem. They also had better interpersonal skills and family relationships and lower levels of anger than low scorers (Tangney, Baumeister, & Boone, 2004).

High self-control is also linked to satisfaction with life, happiness and avoiding frequent conflict (Hofmann, Luhmann, Fisher, Vohs, & Baumeister, 2014).

Parenting matters. In a study of African-American children with an average age of 11.2 years, those whose parents were more nurturing and involved had higher self-control than those whose parents were less so (Wills et al., 2007). In Skinner's terms, this fits the idea that self-control is itself learned from the environment.

Baumeister (quoted in Weir, 2012) noted that self-control had become a 'hot topic'. He argued that most problems of modern society involve self-control failure to some degree, including addiction, overeating, crime, domestic violence, sexually transmitted diseases, prejudice, debt, unwanted pregnancy, underperformance at school and work, lack of savings and failure to exercise.
sections.simple: Research shows that people with high self-control get better grades, are better adjusted, have higher self-esteem, get along better with others and are happier. Children with nurturing, involved parents develop more self-control. Many modern social problems involve failures of self-control.
keyPoints: Tangney, Baumeister & Boone (2004): high self-control students had better grades, adjustment, self-esteem, relationships and less anger.
Hofmann et al. (2014): self-control is linked to life satisfaction, happiness and less conflict.
Wills et al. (2007): nurturing, involved parents produce higher self-control in African-American children (mean age 11.2).
Baumeister: most modern problems (addiction, crime, debt, etc.) involve self-control failure.

sections.heading: Applications of Operant Conditioning: Token Economy Programs
sections.detailed:
Psychologists have applied Skinner's operant-conditioning techniques to change human behavior in clinical, business and educational settings. Behavior modification, a form of therapy that applies the principles of reinforcement to bring about desired behavioral change, has worked with children and adults, with the mentally healthy and the mentally disturbed, and with individuals and groups.

The classic application is the token economy: a behavior-modification technique in which tokens, exchangeable for valued objects or privileges, are awarded for desirable behaviors. In the pioneering study, a ward of female psychotic patients in a state mental institution was run as a giant Skinner box (Ayllon & Azrin, 1968). Conventional treatments could no longer help these patients. They had been institutionalized for a long time and could not care for themselves.

The patients were offered work normally done by paid attendants and earned tokens that functioned like money. Tokens bought goods and privileges: candy, cigarettes, lipstick, gloves and newspapers, a movie on the ward, a walk around the grounds, or a better room. The most expensive privileges, at 100 tokens, were an escorted trip into town and a private meeting with a social worker. A private meeting with a psychologist cost only 20 tokens. Patients earned a token each for bathing at the set time, brushing their teeth, making their beds, combing their hair and dressing properly. They earned up to 10 tokens for each work period in the kitchen or laundry, or for cleaning the ward, running errands or taking other patients for walks.

These tasks look simple, but before the program the patients were considered helpless, aimless and incapable of doing almost anything for themselves. The conditioning worked dramatically. The patients groomed themselves, cleaned their surroundings and kept busy with many tasks. They began interacting socially with each other and with staff, and some even took responsibility for patient care. Their self-esteem improved markedly and they became less dependent.

Token economies have reduced problem behaviors in many institutional settings. Aggressive behavior among cognitively impaired psychiatric patients fell by 79 percent after a nine-month program (DePhilippis et al., 2008). The approach was also highly effective with autistic children in Japan (Ogasahara, Hirono, & Kato, 2013).

The token economy online. Heavy smokers in one study made video recordings of themselves at home twice a day for four weeks. They used a web camera to provide carbon monoxide samples, which were sent electronically to the clinic. They earned vouchers for lowering their carbon monoxide level over a four-day period and for keeping it at a non-smoker's level, and the vouchers could be exchanged for items bought online. The smokers showed significant drops in carbon monoxide and sustained abstinence throughout the study (Dallery, Glenn, & Raiff, 2007).

What happens when the tokens stop? Reinforcement must continue if the changes are to last. When tokens are withdrawn, behaviors usually revert to their original state (Kazdin & Bootzin, 1972; Repucci & Saunders, 1974). However, if caregivers are trained to reward desirable behavior with smiles, praise, hugs and other signs of affection, the behaviors learned in the institution are more likely to continue at home (Kazdin, 1989).
sections.simple: In a token economy, people earn tokens for good behavior and spend them on treats and privileges. In the first study, long-term psychiatric patients who seemed hopeless began caring for themselves, working and socializing. Token systems have also cut aggression, helped autistic children, and even helped smokers quit online. The catch is that behavior slides back when the tokens stop, unless caregivers keep rewarding it with praise and affection.
keyPoints: Behavior modification applies reinforcement principles to produce desired behavior change.
Token economy: tokens earned for desirable behavior are exchanged for goods and privileges.
Ayllon & Azrin (1968): female psychotic patients earned tokens for grooming and work; they became active, social and less dependent.
Later results: 79% drop in aggression (DePhilippis et al., 2008); autistic children in Japan; online vouchers for smokers (Dallery et al., 2007).
Behavior reverts when tokens stop, unless caregivers continue with social reinforcers (Kazdin, 1989).

sections.heading: Behavior Modification Programs
sections.detailed:
Education. Behavior modification has been applied successfully in schools. It has improved academic performance and social behavior in classrooms and reduced behavioral, emotional and developmental problems (Lang & Rispoli, 2015).

Business and industry. Behavior modification programs at major manufacturers, financial institutions and government agencies have reduced absenteeism, lateness and abuse of sick leave, and have improved job performance and safety. The techniques can also be used to teach low-level job skills. Reinforcers used in business include pay, job security, recognition from supervisors, perks and status within the company, and opportunities for personal growth.

What these programs ignore is as important as what they do. They make no attempt to deal with supposed anxieties, repressed traumas or unconscious motives. The focus is entirely on changing overt behavior: defining the appropriate reinforcers and working out the best rate at which to present them. This is Skinner's 'empty organism' principle put into practice.
sections.simple: Behavior modification has improved learning and behavior in schools. In businesses, it has cut absenteeism and lateness and improved performance and safety, using rewards like pay, recognition and status. It works only on visible behavior and ignores inner causes like anxiety or the unconscious.
keyPoints: Education: better academic performance and social behavior; fewer behavioral, emotional and developmental problems (Lang & Rispoli, 2015).
Business: less absenteeism, lateness and sick-leave abuse; better performance and safety; teaching low-level job skills.
Business reinforcers: pay, job security, supervisor recognition, perks and status, personal growth.
Ignores anxieties, repressed traumas and unconscious forces; targets overt behavior, the right reinforcers and their optimal rate.

sections.heading: Punishment and Negative Reinforcement
sections.detailed:
Most operant-conditioning applications use positive reinforcement rather than punishment. The token-economy patients were not punished for failing to behave appropriately. They were reinforced when their behavior improved. Punishment is the application of an aversive stimulus after a response in order to decrease the likelihood that the response will recur.

Skinner held that punishment does not work for changing behavior from undesirable to desirable or from abnormal to normal. Positive reinforcement of desirable behavior is much more effective. In an interview (Goleman, 1987) he argued that punishment works immediately but gives no long-term results. He said people respond to it with an urge to escape, to counterattack, or with stubborn apathy, effects seen in prisons, schools and wherever punishment is used.

Negative reinforcement is not the same as punishment. Negative reinforcement is the strengthening of a response by removing an aversive stimulus. A negative reinforcer is an aversive or noxious stimulus whose removal is rewarding. In a laboratory or classroom, an unpleasant stimulus such as a loud noise or an electric shock can be kept on until the subject emits the desired response. As with positive reinforcement, the environment changes because of the behavior; here the noxious stimulus disappears.

An everyday example: a person may stop smoking to escape the aversive stimulus of a nagging spouse or colleague. The nagging should stop once the desired behavior, not lighting up at home or in the office, appears.

Skinner opposed using noxious stimuli to change behavior. Their consequences are less predictable than those of positive reinforcement, and negative reinforcement does not always work, whereas positive reinforcement is more consistently effective.

Distinguishing the three (a favorite exam question). Positive reinforcement adds something pleasant after a response, so the response becomes more likely. Negative reinforcement removes something unpleasant after a response, so the response also becomes more likely. Punishment adds something unpleasant after a response, so the response becomes less likely. Both kinds of reinforcement strengthen behavior; punishment aims to weaken it.
sections.simple: Skinner preferred positive reinforcement to punishment. Punishment works quickly but does not last, and it makes people want to escape, fight back or stop caring. Negative reinforcement is different from punishment: it strengthens a behavior by taking away something unpleasant, as when a smoker quits so the nagging will stop.
keyPoints: Most applications use positive reinforcement, not punishment.
Punishment: an aversive stimulus after a response, to make it less likely.
Skinner: punishment works immediately but not long term; it produces escape, counterattack or apathy.
Negative reinforcement strengthens a response by removing an aversive stimulus (nagging stops when smoking stops).
Skinner opposed noxious stimuli: results are less predictable, and negative reinforcement is less consistent than positive.

sections.heading: Questions about Human Nature
sections.detailed:
Nature versus nurture. Skinner's position is clear. People are mainly products of learning, shaped more by external variables than by genetic factors.

Childhood versus later experience. We can infer that childhood experiences matter more than later ones, because our basic behaviors are formed in childhood. But behavior can still change in adulthood. What was learned in childhood can be modified, and new behavior patterns can be acquired at any age. The success of behavior-modification programs supports this.

Uniqueness versus universality. Because behavior is shaped by learning, and everyone has different experiences, especially in childhood, each person is unique. No two people behave in exactly the same way.

Ultimate goal. Skinner did not address the idea of a necessary life goal. He made no mention of overcoming inferiority, reducing anxiety or striving for self-actualization, because these assume internal, subjective states that he rejected. Any life goal in his work is societal rather than individual. In Walden Two and elsewhere he described an ideal society and argued that individual behavior should be directed toward the kind of society with the best chance of survival.

Free will versus determinism. Skinner believed people function like machines, in lawful, orderly and predetermined ways. He rejected any idea of an inner being or autonomous self that chooses to act freely and spontaneously. From his scholarly work to his utopian novel, his message was the same: behavior is controlled by reinforcers. In a sense this makes it pointless to blame or punish people. On this view, a dictator who orders mass killings, or a serial killer, is no more responsible than a driverless car rolling down a hill, since both operate lawfully under external control.

Optimism versus pessimism. This does not leave us as helpless, passive robots. Although controlled by the environment, we are responsible for designing that environment. Buildings, cities, consumer goods, factories, media and government institutions are human creations. So are social systems, languages, laws, customs and recreations. We constantly change our environment, often to our advantage, and so we are both controller and controlled: we design the controlling culture and are products of it. Skinner said we may not be free agents but can improve our lives by rearranging the controls on our behavior. His aim, he said, was not to change people but to change the world they live in (quoted in Bjork, 1993).

Summary of his image of human nature: nurture over nature, childhood important but change possible at any age, uniqueness, a societal survival goal, strict determinism, and qualified optimism through environmental design.
sections.simple: Skinner believed people are shaped by learning, not genes. Childhood matters most, but behavior can change at any age, and everyone is unique because their experiences differ. There is no free will: we behave like machines controlled by reinforcers. Still, humans design their own environment, so we can improve our lives by changing it.
keyPoints: Nature–nurture: people are products of learning; external variables matter more than genetics.
Childhood forms basic behaviors, but new patterns can be learned at any age (shown by behavior modification).
Each person is unique because experiences differ.
No individual ultimate goal; the only goal is societal survival (Walden Two).
Strict determinism (people as machines), yet we are both controller and controlled because we design our environment.

sections.heading: Assessment in Skinner's Theory (Direct Observation, Self-Reports, Physiological Measurements)
sections.detailed:
Skinner did not use the usual assessment methods of other theorists. There was no place in his work for free association, dream analysis or projective techniques. Since he was not dealing with personality, he had no interest in assessing it. He did, however, assess behavior.

Before any behavior-modification program, two things must be assessed. The first is the specific behaviors, both desirable and undesirable. The second is the environmental factors that act as reinforcers and can be manipulated to change behavior. No behavior can be properly modified without this prior assessment.

Functional analysis. Skinner's approach to assessing behavior is called functional analysis. It examines three aspects: (1) the frequency of the behavior, (2) the situation in which it occurs, and (3) the reinforcement associated with it. A behavior-modification program cannot be planned until these are known. For example, smokers who want to quit are asked to keep an accurate daily record of how many cigarettes they smoke and in what situations. Does smoking happen in a particular place or at a certain time? With others or alone? After meals or while driving? What are the reinforcers? Most smokers smoke more in the presence of certain stimuli. Identifying these is necessary, because changing the stimuli should change the smoking.

Three approaches. Behavior is assessed through direct observation, self-reports and physiological measurements.

Direct observation. Many behaviors can be observed directly, usually by two or more observers to ensure accuracy and reliability. In a classic case (Hawkins, Peterson, Schweid, & Bijou, 1966), a mother sought help for her unruly 4-year-old son. Two psychologists observed mother and child at home to record the nature and frequency of his undesirable behaviors, when and where they occurred, and what reinforcers he received. They identified nine undesirable behaviors, including kicking, throwing things, biting and pushing a sibling. They saw that the mother gave the boy toys or food when he misbehaved, hoping to make him stop. She was actually rewarding and thus reinforcing the misbehavior. The observation took 16 hours, but without it the psychologists would not have known which behaviors to target or what reinforcers the child expected. The mother was then told to use attention and approval as reinforcers when the child behaved well and never to reward any of the nine undesirable behaviors. The frequencies recorded during observation provided a baseline against which behavior during and after treatment could be compared.

Self-reports. Interviews and questionnaires ask people to observe and report on their own behavior. For example, a questionnaire might assess how much fear a person feels when driving, going to the dentist or speaking in public. These questionnaires are similar in format to self-report personality inventories.

Physiological measurements. Heart rate, muscle tension and brain waves can be recorded to evaluate the physiological effects of various stimuli. They can also confirm the accuracy of information from other methods. A person too embarrassed to admit a fear of elevators in an interview or questionnaire might still show a change in heart rate or muscle tension when asked about elevators.

Whatever technique is used, the focus stays on what people do, not on what might have motivated them. The ultimate goal is to modify behavior, not to change personality.
sections.simple: Skinner did not assess personality, only behavior. His functional analysis asks how often a behavior happens, in what situations, and what reinforces it. Behavior is measured by directly watching it, by asking people to report on themselves, or by recording body signals like heart rate. The goal is always to change behavior, not personality.
keyPoints: No free association, dream analysis or projective tests; Skinner assessed behavior, not personality.
Functional analysis: frequency of the behavior, situation in which it occurs, and its reinforcers.
Direct observation, usually by two or more observers; Hawkins et al. (1966) found a mother was reinforcing her son's nine misbehaviors.
Self-reports via interviews and questionnaires (e.g., fear of driving, the dentist, public speaking).
Physiological measures (heart rate, muscle tension, brain waves) evaluate stimulus effects and check other methods.

sections.heading: Research on Skinner's Theory
sections.detailed:
Skinner's research methods differed from mainstream experimental psychology as much as his assessment methods differed from other theorists'. The usual procedure is to study large groups of animal or human subjects and compare their average responses statistically. Skinner instead preferred the intensive study of a single subject.

His reasons were these. Data on the average performance of a group are of little value in dealing with a particular case. A science built on averages offers little help in understanding the unique individual. Skinner believed that valid and replicable results could be obtained without statistical analysis, as long as enough data were collected from a single subject under well-controlled experimental conditions. Large groups force the experimenter to deal with average behavior. The resulting data cannot reflect individual response behavior or individual differences.

Skinner and his followers conducted thousands of operant-conditioning experiments on topics such as reinforcement schedules, language acquisition, behavior shaping, superstitious behavior and behavior modification. The results have been highly supportive of his ideas.

Research highlights from the chapter: (1) greater reinforcement during training makes a conditioned response more resistant to extinction; (2) operant conditioning can shape most forms of behavior in humans and animals; (3) even a lobster can be conditioned; (4) American major league players show more superstitious behavior than Japanese players; (5) college students high in self-control get better grades, are better adjusted and have higher self-esteem; (6) token economies have cut aggression in cognitively impaired patients by as much as 79 percent.
sections.simple: Most psychologists study large groups and compare averages with statistics. Skinner instead studied one subject in great detail, because averages say little about any single individual. Thousands of experiments by Skinner and his followers have strongly supported his ideas.
keyPoints: Mainstream research compares group averages statistically; Skinner preferred intensive study of a single subject.
Group averages are of little value for a particular case or the unique individual.
Valid, replicable results are possible without statistics, given enough data under well-controlled conditions.
Thousands of experiments on schedules, language, shaping, superstition and behavior modification have been highly supportive.

sections.heading: Reflections on Skinner's Theory
sections.detailed:
Criticisms. Those who oppose determinism find much to dislike in Skinner. Humanistic psychologists, who see people as more complex than machines, rats or pigeons, object to his image of human nature. They argue that focusing only on overt behavior ignores uniquely human qualities such as conscious free will.

Critics also question his choice of subjects and the simplicity of his experimental situations. Skinner made broad, confident claims about human behavior and society, covering social, economic, religious and cultural issues. Critics ask whether one can really extrapolate from a pigeon pecking a disc to a person functioning in the real world. The gap seems too vast for such broad generalizations, and many aspects of human behavior cannot be meaningfully reduced to the level at which Skinner worked. The chapter summary also mentions criticism of his lack of interest in any behavior other than response rate.

Instinctive drift. Skinner's belief that all behavior is learned was challenged by two of his former students, Breland and Breland. They conditioned more than 6,000 animals of 38 species, including pigs, raccoons, chickens, hamsters, porpoises, whales and cows, to perform in television commercials and tourist attractions. The animals showed instinctive drift: they substituted instinctive behaviors for the behaviors that had been reinforced, even when this interfered with getting food. For example, pigs and raccoons were trained to pick up a coin, carry it some distance and drop it into a toy piggy bank, earning food after a certain number of coins. They learned quickly, but after a while the pigs began burying the coin and rooting it out with their snouts, and the raccoons spent a long time rubbing it with washing-like movements (Richelle, 1993). Instinctive behavior took precedence over learned behavior, even though it delayed reinforcement. Commercially it was a disaster. The trainers' article, "The Misbehavior of Organisms" (Breland & Breland, 1961), parodied the title of Skinner's book The Behavior of Organisms (1938) and reportedly displeased him (Gillaspy, 2009).

Skinner's response. He ignored most criticism. He once said of a critic's review that he read a bit, saw the critic had missed the point, and had better things to do than correct misunderstandings (quoted in Rice, 1968). Asked how he coped with being misunderstood so often, he said he needed to be understood only three or four times a year (quoted in Blackman, 1995).

Contributions and recognition. Skinner was a potent force in 20th-century American psychology and perhaps shaped the field more than anyone else. The Journal of the Experimental Analysis of Behavior, begun in 1958, publishes research on individual subjects. The Journal of Applied Behavior Analysis was founded in 1968 for work on behavior-modification techniques. He received the American Psychological Foundation's Gold Medal and the APA's Distinguished Scientific Contribution Award (1958). Its citation praised his profound impact on psychology and on promising younger psychologists. His first book, The Behavior of Organisms: An Experimental Analysis (1938), was described as one of the few books to truly change the field (Thompson, 1988). He also received the U.S. National Medal of Science and appeared on the cover of Time as the world's most famous American psychologist. His controversial Beyond Freedom and Dignity (1971) became a best seller. It made him a celebrity on talk shows, swamped with mail, calls and visits, and asked by strangers to shake his hand in restaurants (Bjork, 1993).
sections.simple: Critics say Skinner treated people like machines, ignored free will, and generalized too far from simple animal experiments. His own former students, the Brelands, found that trained animals drift back to instinctive behaviors, which showed that not everything is learned. Skinner mostly ignored critics. He was still one of the most influential and famous psychologists of the 20th century.
keyPoints: Criticized by opponents of determinism and by humanists for ignoring conscious free will and uniquely human qualities.
Critics question generalizing from simple animal experiments (a pigeon pecking a disc) to complex human society.
Instinctive drift (Breland & Breland, 1961): animals replaced reinforced behaviors with instinctive ones, challenging 'all behavior is learned'.
Skinner ignored most criticism ('understood only three or four times a year').
Honors: APA Distinguished Scientific Contribution Award (1958), APF Gold Medal, National Medal of Science, Time cover; two journals founded.

sections.heading: Current Status
sections.detailed:
Skinner's radical behaviorism is still applied in laboratory, clinical and organizational settings. However, its dominance has been challenged by the cognitive movement in psychology, which began in the 1960s. Skinner himself admitted that his kind of psychology had lost ground to the cognitive approach. Other psychologists agreed. Baars (1986) wrote that Skinnerian behaviorism had fallen from favor with most active researchers and was often referred to in the past tense.

Despite these inroads by cognitive psychology, Skinner's position remains influential in many areas: classrooms, assembly lines, Skinner boxes and treatment programs for behavior disorders. Skinner believed that operant conditioning offered a technique for improving human nature and the societies people design.

For exam answers on the impact of cognitive psychology: the cognitive movement reinstated the inner mental processes that Skinner excluded, and it displaced radical behaviorism as the dominant approach. Behaviorism's applied techniques, especially behavior modification, nonetheless remain popular and effective.
sections.simple: Since the 1960s, cognitive psychology, which studies the mind, has pushed Skinner's behaviorism out of first place, and even Skinner admitted it. But his methods are still widely used in schools, workplaces and therapy programs.
keyPoints: Radical behaviorism is still applied in laboratory, clinical and organizational settings.
The cognitive movement (from the 1960s) challenged and overtook its dominance; Skinner conceded this.
Baars (1986): behaviorism had fallen from favor and was often spoken of in the past tense.
Still influential in classrooms, assembly lines, Skinner boxes and treatment of behavior disorders.

terms.definition: Skinner's approach of studying only overt, observable behavior and explaining it by external consequences, without reference to inner states.
Skinner's description of humans: nothing inside the organism (mental or physiological) can explain behavior in scientific terms.
Responses made to, or elicited by, specific environmental stimuli, such as a reflexive knee jerk.
Learned respondent behavior in which one stimulus comes to substitute for another, as when Pavlov's dogs salivated to a bell.
Strengthening a response by adding a reward, which makes the response more likely to be repeated.
Eliminating a behavior by withholding reinforcement.
Behavior emitted spontaneously or voluntarily that operates on the environment and changes it.
Elicited behavior is drawn out by a specific stimulus (respondent); emitted behavior occurs with no identifiable stimulus (operant).
The procedure by which changing the consequences of a response affects the rate at which the response occurs.
Skinner's operant-conditioning apparatus, in which a rat's lever press delivers a food pellet.
Presenting a reinforcer after every response.
Patterns or rates of providing or withholding reinforcers.
Reinforcement for the first response after a fixed time period has elapsed, regardless of the number of responses (e.g., a monthly salary).
Reinforcement only after a specified number of responses (e.g., piece-rate pay, commission).
Reinforcement after time periods that vary from one reinforcement to the next (e.g., fishing).
Reinforcement after a number of responses that varies around an average (e.g., slot machines); produces high, stable, extinction-resistant responding.
Reinforcing only some responses; responses reinforced this way take longer to extinguish than continuously reinforced ones.
Explanation of how complex behavior is acquired: behavior is reinforced only as it comes closer to the final desired behavior.
Giving stronger or more selective reinforcement to responses closer to the target, as when parents shape speech in stages.
Persistent behavior that has a coincidental, not functional, relationship to the reinforcement received.
